title: Next Greater Element
statement: Given an array nums, return an array where result[i] is the first element to the right of i that is strictly greater than nums[i], or -1 if there is none. In the two-array variant, nums1 is a subset of nums2 and you must answer the same question for each element of nums1 using its position in nums2.
realWorld: Order books ask it constantly: for a resting bid, what is the next price above it in the stream? Log and metric pipelines ask the same question as 'when does this series next exceed its current level', which is the basis of threshold and breakout detection.

examples.explanation: The 2 at index 0 is beaten by the 4 at index 3 — not by the 2 at index 2, because the comparison is strict. The 4 and the trailing 3 are never beaten.
Solve nums2 once, storing value -> next-greater in a map, then look up each element of nums1. This works only because nums2's values are distinct, which the variant guarantees.
Nothing is ever popped. All five indices sit on the stack at the end and all five keep the -1 sentinel.

constraints: In the two-array variant all values of nums2 are distinct and nums1 is a subset of nums2

bruteForce.whySlow: On a descending array every index scans to the end and finds nothing, giving n(n-1)/2 comparisons — 5 x 10^9 at n = 10^5. Every one of those scans re-reads values a previous scan already rejected, and nothing is learned from a rejection.

patternIdentification: This is the definition of the monotonic-stack pattern rather than an application of it: the answer for i is the *nearest* qualifying element on one side. The key realisation is that once an element is beaten, it can be discarded forever — anything further right that would have chosen it prefers the element that beat it, which is both larger and closer.

optimized.idea: Sweep left to right keeping a stack of indices whose answer is still unknown, with values decreasing from bottom to top. Each arrival pops every index it beats and becomes their answer. Indices still on the stack at the end never met anything larger, so they keep -1.

complexity.space: O(n) for the stack, plus O(n) for the value map in the two-array form

res[stack.pop()] = nums[i];   // i is the answer for that waiting index
stack.push(i);                    // nothing bigger yet — wait here
return res;                           // whatever is still waiting stays -1

commonMistakes: Pushing values rather than indices. It happens to work for this exact problem because the answer is a value, but it breaks the moment you need a distance or a width, and it makes the two-array mapping harder than it needs to be.
Using `<=` in the pop condition, which makes an equal value count as 'greater'. On [2,1,2,4,3] that wrongly answers index 0 with 2 instead of 4.
Building the map from nums1 instead of nums2 in the two-array variant — the stack sweep must run over nums2, which is the array that defines the order.
Assuming the value-keyed map works in general. It relies on nums2's values being distinct; with duplicates you must key by index instead.
Forgetting the circular follow-up's trick: walk 2n indices using i % n and push only while i < n, so every element gets a full lap without being queued twice.
